input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Motivate the challenge of reliable long-form scientific writing with large language models, state the research question—how does graph-guided sectioning affect coherence and citation quality?—and give a high-level overview of the graph-guided prompting workflow and conservative claim policy (always cite sources).

output:
General background knowledge: practitioners and reviewers have raised concerns about the reliability of long-form scientific text produced by contemporary language models, in particular with respect to factual support, citation consistency, and ease of post-hoc verification. These concerns motivate methods that prioritize explicit evidence grounding and machine-checkable outputs when applying automated or semi-automated writing workflows to scholarly manuscripts.

This work asks a focused research question: how does encoding document structure as an explicit section-level graph and using that graph to guide evidence-aware, JSON-constrained generation affect the coherence of section composition and the fidelity of citations in long-form scientific writing? We frame the question narrowly to evaluate whether a graph-guided scheduling and prompting workflow can (a) increase the proportion of section claims that are directly supported by retrieved evidence and (b) make unsupported assertions easier to detect and correct during later audits.

To answer this question we introduce a graph-aware prompting workflow that (1) represents a draft manuscript as a document graph whose nodes are sections and whose directed edges encode prerequisite and dependency relations between sections; (2) uses a leaf-first scheduling algorithm to order section generation so that sections with fewer downstream dependents are written first; (3) retrieves and ranks candidate evidence for each section and injects the top-ranked items into section-specific prompts; (4) constrains the model outputs to a strict, machine-checked JSON schema that requires explicit citation anchors for factual assertions and separates prose from structured metadata; and (5) assembles validated JSON section artifacts into a LaTeX manuscript with an accompanying refs.bib file. The workflow is designed so that each generated section is an auditable unit: the JSON artifact contains the section text, the list of evidence items used, and discrete fields for claims that require citation. The assembly step applies conservative validation checks (e.g., citation coverage thresholds, simple unsupported-claim heuristics) and logs failures for human review.

We evaluate the proposed workflow against a baseline linear prompting pipeline using two topical domains drawn from internal notes and a small curated set of PDFs where available. Evaluation focuses on citation coverage, rate of unsupported assertions identified by annotators, and reviewer-style assessments of local coherence and usefulness. Consistent with the design goals, we adopt a conservative reporting policy: empirical claims are limited to the evaluated settings, and all factual assertions in generated text are required to include explicit source citations. We do not claim broad generalization beyond the experiment domains; limitations and failure modes are discussed later in the paper.

Contributions of this paper are threefold: (i) a document-graph construction and leaf-first scheduling procedure for section-level generation; (ii) an evidence-injection and JSON-constrained prompting protocol that enforces source-first writing and facilitates automatic validation; and (iii) an audit-oriented assembly process that produces a LaTeX manuscript plus refs.bib while retaining per-section provenance for downstream review and editing. We emphasize conservative interpretation of results and present the workflow primarily as a reproducible, audit-friendly approach for improving citation fidelity in model-assisted scientific writing.
